entries.name: Alustriel's Arcana
entries: In this book, the archmage Alustriel Silverhand from the Forgotten Realms setting—a human daughter of the god of magic Mystra and paragon of righteousness and virtue—presents arcana she has discovered during her travels. (You can learn more about Alustriel in {@adventure Vecna: Eve of Ruin.|VEoR|13|Alustriel Silverhand})

But the contents of this book can be used in any setting, whether it's the Forgotten Realms, Ravenloft, or one of your own making. Think of this book as a toy box full of options to incorporate into your game as the Dungeon Master chooses.
This book relies on the rules in the {@book Player's Handbook, |XPHB}{@book Dungeon Master's Guide,|XDMG} and {@book Monster Manual.|XMM}

entries.name: Schools of Magic
entries: The eight schools of magic that underlie spellcraft are key to this book's magical character options, and its magical factions and tools for building magical worlds are tied to the schools' nuanced characteristics. The following entries expand on the schools' brief descriptions in the {@book Player's Handbook:|XPHB|7|School of Magic}

items: {@b Abjuration} spells include protective and healing magic, as well as magic that prevents or reverses unwanted effects.
{@b Conjuration} spells involve creating objects and effects, summoning creatures, or teleporting.
{@b Divination} spells allow the caster to peer into the future or other planes of existence to gain helpful or bolstering benefits or information.
{@b Enchantment} spells include magic that bends targets' minds to the caster's will.
{@b Evocation} spells create physical effects that are often spectacular and might include destructive energy such as fire, cold, and acid.
{@b Illusion} spells include magic that creates sounds, images, smells, and other sensory effects that deceive the mind or senses.
{@b Necromancy} spells manipulate life and death, including restoring the dead to life, animating undead creatures, and siphoning life from the living.
{@b Transmutation} spells include magic that transforms creatures and objects, granting characteristics and abilities they previously lacked.

entries.name: Using This Book
entries: Chapters 1 and 2 include character creation and play options and are suitable for all players; the remainder of this book is intended for DMs only. The chapters cover the following topics:

items: {@book Chapter 1: Character Options.|AU|1} This chapter presents eight subclasses, ten backgrounds, and more than two dozen feats perfect for creating characters who inhabit a magical world.
{@book Chapter 2: Spells.|AU|2} Dozens of spells offer new options for spellcasting heroes.

{@book Chapter 3: Creating Magical Worlds.|AU|3} This chapter presents guidelines for making magic a central part of your game, with examples from D&D settings, and examples of magical group patrons to inspire your games in any high-magic realm.
Chapter 4: Magical Factions. Nine organizations of magic aficionados—one affiliated with each school of magic, plus one magical saboteur group—provide powerful allies or fearsome foes.
{@book Chapter 5: Magic Items.|AU|5} This chapter presents myriad new magic items to fill your magical hoards, plus rules for magic items that grow in power alongside the player characters.

{@book Chapter 6: Magical Creatures.|AU|6} This bestiary includes statistics for eight specialized archmages, minions warped by foul magic, living spells, the fiendish villain known as {@creature Venger|AU}, and more.
{@book Appendix: Tomb of the Shadow Serpents.|AU|7} This adventure for level 1 characters presents a challenge from {@creature Venger|AU} to claim treasure or die trying.

entries.title: Alustriel Silverhand invites you to peruse the arcana she has discovered.

entries.name: The Weave of Magic
entries: The worlds within the D&D multiverse are magical places. All existence is suffused with magical power, and potential energy lies untapped in every rock, stream, and living creature—even in the air itself. Raw magic is present in every manifestation of energy throughout the multiverse.

Mortals can't directly shape this raw magic. Instead, they use a fabric of magic—an interface between the will of a spellcaster and raw magic. The spellcasters of the Forgotten Realms call it the Weave and recognize its essence as the god Mystra, but casters have varied ways of naming and conceptualizing this interface.

Whenever a magic effect is created, the threads of the Weave intertwine, twist, and fold to make the effect possible. A spellcaster surrounded by the Weave can shape lightning to blast foes, transport hundreds of miles in the blink of an eye, or even reverse death.

But in places where the Weave is damaged, magic works in unpredictable ways—and if it's torn, raw magic is inaccessible. Even the most powerful archmage can't light a candle via magic in an area where the Weave has been torn.
My Esteemed Heroes,
Magic thrums through our multiverse. Powerful magic can save or destroy worlds, though magic's balance is as delicate as a thread.
For centuries, as a daughter of the goddess of magic Mystra, I have protected the Weave and fostered the good in all creatures, lest wickedness snap the Weave.

This has happened more than once, and the resulting suffering was immense. To prevent the unthinkable, magic must cultivate love, joy, and hope and banish hatred and pain. While I draw breath, I shall pursue this cause.
My friends—heroes—I hope you will join me.
However, I know you can't join my cause without knowledge of magic's greatest wonders. And so I bequeath in this tome arcana I have collected throughout my long life.
I hope you use this arcana to better your worlds, but I can't make that choice for you. I simply reveal the gifts of my divine mother and trust you will use them to do good.
May Mystra smile on you always,

data.name: Chapter 1: Character Options

entries.title: When magic is involved, a hero's journey can take infinite paths.

entries: This chapter is full of new character options you can use to make characters suited to magical settings. The pages that follow include new and revised subclasses, new backgrounds, and new feats.

entries.name: Subclasses
entries: This chapter presents eight new subclasses that are particularly appropriate for characters in settings that emphasize magic:

items: {@class Cleric|XPHB|Arcana Domain (Cleric)|Arcana|AU}: A Cleric of a divine force who understands the secrets and potential of magic intimately
{@class Fighter|XPHB|Arcane Archer (Fighter)|Arcane Archer|AU}: A Fighter who draws on a unique tradition of elven archery to weave magic into their attacks
{@class Monk|XPHB|Warrior of the Mystic Arts (Monk)|Mystic Arts|AU}: A Monk who wields magic to supplement their martial skill
{@class Warlock|XPHB|Vestige Patron (Warlock)|Vestige|AU}: A Warlock who draws on the power of a dying god
{@class Wizard|XPHB|Conjurer (Wizard)|Conjurer|AU}: A Wizard who has mastered the arts of teleportation and summoning spirit allies
{@class Wizard|XPHB|Enchanter (Wizard)|Enchanter|AU}: A Wizard who has become an expert in clouding and captivating minds
{@class Wizard|XPHB|Necromancer (Wizard)|Necromancer|AU}: A Wizard who can manipulate and draw magic from life, death, and undeath
{@class Wizard|XPHB|Transmuter (Wizard)|Transmuter|AU}: A Wizard who has mastered modifying energy and matter

entries: Mystra's gifts range from subtle to earthshakingly powerful. Infuse your day with a little magic or stop a mighty villain from causing suffering—or both. When you study magic, your options are unlimited.

entries.name: Backgrounds
entries: This section presents ten backgrounds using the same format as those in the {@book Player's Handbook|XPHB|4|Background Descriptions}. These backgrounds are listed in the Backgrounds table. Descriptions of the Origin feats granted by each background can be found later in this chapter.

Nine of these backgrounds connect characters to magical factions presented in chapter 4. These backgrounds describe the training associated with a faction but aren't required for affiliation with or membership in that faction.
The tenth background, {@background Familiar Trainer|AU}, supports any character who grew up with a magical animal companion.

data.name: Chapter 3: Creating Magical Worlds

entries.title: In highly magical worlds, people use magic for major tasks such as construction.

entries: Using the advice and tools in this chapter, you can create your own world infused with magic for your D&D games. This chapter also provides guidelines for tailoring a group patron for your characters' adventures, helping the players feel immersed in your setting. When creating your magical world, you can choose the options you like best or modify an existing world using your favorite advice. For example, you could use an archmage group patron of your own creation in your adventures that take place in the Forgotten Realms.

entries.name: Magic in Existing Worlds
entries: If you want to use this chapter's advice within an existing world, consider the ones on the D&D Settings table. It describes the magic prevalent in each setting as well as where you can find more information about those settings.

entries.name: Building a Magical World
entries: The advice presented here will help you build your own magical world. Each of the sections that follow focuses on a different aspect of world-building, beginning with the broadest concepts and proceeding to specific topics, including questions designed to guide your creativity. Examples from throughout the D&D multiverse illustrate approaches to each of these subjects:

entries.caption: D&D Settings
rows: Draconic magic is a major theme in this setting consumed by war. The use of magic granted by gods is rare.
{@adventure Dragonlance: Shadow of the Dragon Queen|DSotDQ}
Magic is ubiquitous and functions like technology, providing services such as rapid transportation and long-distance communication.
{@book Eberron: Forge of the Artificer|EFA} and {@book Eberron: Rising from the Last War|ERLW}
Many types of magic infuse dozens of realms. The gods walk in disguise among mortals.
{@book Forgotten Realms: Heroes of Faerûn|FRHoF} and {@book Forgotten Realms: Adventures in Faerûn|FRAiF}
Magic is widespread and commonly used but still wondrous and sometimes frightening.
Magical mists ensure each domain is a prison for its magical Darklord, or ruler, and the hapless residents here. Magic here is ominous and scary.
{@book Ravenloft: The Horrors Within|RHW} and {@adventure Curse of Strahd|CoS}

items: {@area Outline Your World.|138|x} Which types of magic and realms exist in your world?
{@area Attitudes Toward Magic.|13f|x} How do people in your realms view magic and its use?
{@area Religion.|142|x} What gods of magic exist?
{@area Technology.|14b|x} Does technology also exist, and if so, how do magic and technology interact?
{@area Laws.|150|x} Do laws regulate or encourage the use of magic?
{@area Commerce.|156|x} How does the business of spellcasting and magic items function, and are mages' guilds prominent?
{@area Magical Armies.|15e|x} How do the use and prevalence of magic affect warfare and the forces used to fight it?

entries: Magical worlds beyond the dreams of the most learned scholars hold limitless knowledge. Mystra willing, you might master their gifts. Use this power wisely, friends.

entries.name: Outline Your World

entries.title: Performers infuse their music with magic to create a joyous environment.

entries: Before you create individual realms and societies, determine basic details about magic in your world. Consider which categories of magic are most or least prevalent, how that magic shaped the world's geography, and the nature of the major realms.

entries.name: Categories of Magic
entries: In the worlds of D&D, magic can be categorized in three main ways: by different approaches (arcane or divine), by the schools of magic, and by distinct magical traditions. You might use any of these categories to define the role of magic in your world.

entries.name: Approaches to Magic
entries: The spells of Bards, Sorcerers, Warlocks, and Wizards are commonly called arcane magic. These practitioners rely on direct apprehension of the laws and principles of magic. Wizards study those principles directly, Sorcerers and Bards have a more intuitive understanding, and Warlocks gain that knowledge through their pacts.

The spells of Clerics, Druids, Paladins, and Rangers are called divine magic, though the nature magic of Druids and Rangers is sometimes divided into its own category: primal magic. All these practitioners approach magic mediated by gods, the forces of nature, the sacred weight of a Paladin's oath, or some other divine force.

entries.name: Schools of Magic
entries: The eight schools of magic are Abjuration, Conjuration, Divination, Enchantment, Evocation, Illusion, Necromancy, and Transmutation. These schools represent the underpinnings of all magic in a D&D world. All D&D spells belong to one of these schools.

In your world, spellcasters might experience sensory effects when casting spells of different schools. For example, their scalps might tingle while casting Evocation spells, they might see flashes of events in their peripheral vision while casting Divination spells, or they might smell the phantom scent of grave soil while casting Necromancy spells.

entries.name: Magical Traditions
entries: Spellcasters of any sort might practice a wide variety of magical traditions. Dragons claim to be the originators of magic on some worlds. Some magical traditions rely entirely on rituals (which characters can access through the {@variantrule Ritual|XPHB} Caster feat in the {@book Player's Handbook|XPHB}). Rune magic (discussed in {@book Bigby Presents: Glory of the Giants|BGG}) was pioneered by giants and represents a distinct magical tradition. In the Forgotten Realms setting, ancient elves developed the tradition of high magic and used it to transform the world. Spellcasters in that setting also developed the practice of Circle magic (detailed in {@book Forgotten Realms: Heroes of Faerûn|FRHoF}), which allows spellcasters to pool their efforts to cast powerful spells. Magical traditions can also be passed down through family lines, as is the case with Eberron's dragonmarks—magical birthmarks that grant the use of specific spells (as described in {@book Eberron: Forge of the Artificer|EFA}).

entries.name: Magical Geography
entries: Think about the ways magic has shaped the physical landscape of your world. Perhaps a powerful archmage, desiring privacy, used magic to raise mountains around her home. Or a nation governed by powerful mages might cloak the realm in protective magic to block its enemies' magical prying. Your world might boast enormous monuments or strange geographical features created by magic in eons long gone or left behind by the gods in an ancient war.

Magic can have more modest effects too, which nonetheless impact the daily life of your world's residents. For example, in Calimport in the Forgotten Realms, a magical lake inside the city supplies water for residents, while a floating tower serves as headquarters for soldiers who ride flying carpets. The more common magic is in your setting, the more visible its effects should be throughout the world.

entries.name: Magical Realms
entries: As you think about your world's geography, consider the realms within it. Are they all home to powerful spellcasters? Are some more reliant on magic than others?

Your world might include three realms that each rely on a different type of magic. For example, one realm is ruled by wizards who each focus on a particular school of magic. In contrast, another realm is the domain of warlocks who gain their powers from a mysterious, otherworldly entity, while the third realm is ruled by sorcerers who descend from dragons and those who worshipped them. This emphasis on different kinds of spellcasting in each realm gives each a distinct flavor and culture.

On the other hand, you might find it useful to have realms in your world that don't emphasize magic to serve as a contrast to the realms that do. A small realm surrounded by warlike neighbors with large armies of ordinary soldiers, for example, might turn to magic to defend itself and become a haven for mages.

entries.name: Attitudes Toward Magic
entries: Once you've determined the types of magic that pervade your world, consider how your world's inhabitants view magic. Do they welcome magic and the potential it represents? Or do they resent and fear magic, seeing it as a force for unexpected change and danger? Do attitudes vary by region?

entries.name: Trust in or Distrust of Magic
entries: A society that has relied on magic for generations has likely grown accustomed to magic's effects on daily life. Such societies' traditions and practices take magic into account. If access to the {@spell Find Familiar|XPHB} spell is common, for example, public spaces and businesses would be designed to accommodate familiars as well as people.

Alternatively, a society might distrust magic that's not a part of daily life. Perhaps an unfamiliar kind of magic is blamed for a memorable tragedy, leading people to distrust that type of magic. For example, a realm that's been invaded by an army of undead might prohibit necromancy even if the realm encourages other schools of magic.

entries.name: Magical Shortcuts
entries: Magic can often accomplish tasks more quickly and easily than is normally possible. While people in a magic-rich society easily accept the convenience and reliability of magical substitutes for common services, there might be a backlash effect or unusual side effects from folk taking magic for granted.
For example, wealthy nobles might seek out a chef capable of making food "the old-fashioned way." Or a society rife with healing magic might become obsessed with thrill-seeking and dangerous sports.

entries.name: Religion
entries: Most D&D worlds have many gods, and a magical society usually has at least one god of magic.
Are there gods of magic in your world? Who are they? What do they expect of their worshippers and from individuals who wield magic? Are they benevolent, antagonistic, or ambivalent toward mortals?

entries.name: Benevolent Magic Gods
entries: You might include a benevolent god of magic in your world. Such a god believes magic should be used for good, improving the lives of ordinary people. They encourage teaching and promoting the use of magic, and aspiring mages are expected to maintain a moral and ethical code that emphasizes selflessness, duty, and charity.

For example, crafters in a world with a benevolent god of magic are encouraged to make Common magic items that benefit others. When adventurers recover lost magic from ancient dungeons, priests hide dangerous magic away while they share useful magic with as many people as possible.

Including a benevolent god of magic in your world doesn't preclude the inclusion of evil mages. Indeed, a benevolent god of magic might be outnumbered or outmatched by evil rivals. This prompts the god of magic or their followers to seek help from the characters.

entries.name: Mystra
entries: Mystra is a benevolent god of magic in the Forgotten Realms setting. Mystra has been destroyed or defeated multiple times, but each time she has returned in a new form with the help of brave adventurers.

entries.name: Antagonistic Magic Gods
entries: A god of magic might spread evil, cruelty, and tyranny through the use of magic. An antagonistic god of magic favors nefarious uses of magic. Such a god's necromancer followers might raise large armies of undead to unleash on the population. Or adherents might use powerful Evocation spells to destroy rival cities and those who live in them. An antagonistic god of magic might rule a realm dedicated to evil and populated with undead, devils or demons, and other bloodthirsty creatures.

entries.name: Iuz and Vecna
entries: The demigod Iuz, described in the {@book Dungeon Master's Guide|XDMG}, and {@book Vecna|XDMG|8|Vecna}, whose schemes to amass ultimate power are described in {@adventure Vecna: Eve of Ruin|VEoR}, are both antagonistic gods who seek conquest through magic. Iuz is primarily a god of deceit and oppression, but his methods involve seeking ancient magic he can use to increase his power. Vecna plots from the shadows and reveals himself only when victory is nigh.

entries.name: Ambivalent Magic Gods
entries: A god of magic might be ambivalent about their followers. Such a deity cares more about whether magic is used than about how it is used. When characters recover lost magical secrets during an adventure, an ambivalent god of magic might want those magical secrets locked away and preserved—not out of a selfish desire to control the information, but out of an intellectual interest in ensuring this knowledge isn't lost again.

entries.name: Mystryl
entries: An ambivalent god of magic might guard the source of all magic or even embody magic. Mystryl, the original god of magic in the Forgotten Realms, embodied magic in this way. When Mystryl died, magic was transformed; spellcasting became unreliable, and spellcasters lost their ability to cast their most powerful spells. Magic stabilized only when the god of magic returned as Mystra.

entries.name: Boccob
entries: An ambivalent god of magic in the Greyhawk setting and patron of the legendary mage {@book Mordenkainen|XDMG|8|Mordenkainen}, Boccob works to ensure that good and evil forces remain equal.

entries.name: Weaving a Divine Tapestry
entries: A high-magic setting might include multiple gods of magic, each with conflicting goals and methods. No single god is likely to completely satisfy a society ruled by mages where spellcasting is common. Including multiple competing gods of magic gives your players more choices for patron gods for their characters. The conflict between rival gods of magic can create adventures and drive campaigns.

Your world might have different gods for each school of magic (a god of Conjuration, for example, and a god of Transmutation). Or a primary god of magic might be assisted by other gods, each with their own emphasis. For example, Mystra is assisted by Azuth, a god of wizardry who is ambivalent in his outlook and uninterested in the moral and ethical use of magic.

Your world might even have no god focused entirely on magic. In a world where magic suffuses every aspect of life, every god might carry some responsibility for the use of magic as it impacts the rest of their portfolio. A god of war cares not just about weapons and bloodshed, but about the use of magic in battle. A god of crafting might have dominion over making magic items and over artisans who use magic in their trades. And a god of knowledge might govern the academic study of magic often associated with gods of magic. Eberron's pantheon is a good example.

entries.name: Technology
entries: Many D&D campaigns assume the technology of a medieval or early renaissance setting. However, the {@book Dungeon Master's Guide|XDMG} has rules for modern firearms and futuristic weapons such as {@item Antimatter Rifle|XDMG|Antimatter Rifles} and {@item Laser Pistol|XDMG|Laser Pistols}. Further examples of futuristic technology can be found in {@adventure Quests from the Infinite Staircase|QftIS}.

When you create your magical world, consider what level of technology is present. Does advanced technology exist in your setting? If it does, what do people think of it? Is technology a replacement for or a supplement to magic?

entries.name: Technological Revolution
entries: To introduce more advanced technology into your world, you can present it as originating in a recent technological revolution. An ancient and magic-focused realm ruled by mages might suddenly discover technological innovation. This could streamline daily life with simple technology, such as long-range communications, and add options for characters who like technology. It could also threaten the realm's rulers and therefore lead to technology being heavily regulated. Threatened rulers might hunt down inventors and destroy their creations. On the flip side, rulers might feel threatened by magic-users, leading these rulers to embrace technology to stave off power-hungry mages.

entries.name: Rival Powers

entries.title: In Eberron, magic mimics technology, allowing wonders such as airships.

entries: Alternatively, you can introduce technology to your world by creating a rival realm that relies on technology much like your magical society relies on magic. These two realms could be equivalent in wealth, status, and influence, but what one accomplishes with spells, the other achieves through machines.

Consider whether characters might come from either realm, or if the entire party hails from one society or the other. The first case encourages wildly different characters; some heroes enter battle with the {@spell Magic Missile|XPHB} and {@spell Fireball|XPHB} spells prepared, while others rely on their trusty {@item Laser Pistol|XDMG|Laser Pistols} and {@item Grenade Launcher|XDMG|Grenade Launchers}.

If all characters come from one of the realms, the other society can serve as a rival and antagonist. If, for example, all your characters are from a magical society bordering a high-technology realm, tension between these two lands runs high and conflict is inevitable. Your campaign might begin with the characters infiltrating their technologically advanced neighbor while concealing their magical skills. There, the characters discover a plan for a mechanical army to invade the party's homeland. To thwart this invasion, the characters need to lead a force of conjured creatures, undead, and other magical warriors.

entries.name: Magic and Technology in Tandem
entries: Magic and technology need not be oppositional forces. You can create a society in which magic and technology operate side by side. In such a realm, bandits are just as likely to cast the {@spell Fire Bolt|XPHB} spell as they are to draw a {@item Laser Pistol|XDMG}. Citizens predict the weather with the {@spell Druidcraft|XPHB} spell, but they tell time using a clock in the middle of town.

entries.name: Eberron
entries: In a variant of this approach, magic provides the power for technology. Magic is used this way in Eberron. Eberron has airships, trains, and other examples of industrial technology, but these devices are powered by spells, magic items, and Elementals instead of nonmagical batteries and engines. Instantaneous, long-distance communication is possible in Eberron through {@item Sending Stones|XDMG} staffed by members of a dragonmarked house; the result is akin to a magical telegraph network. Similarly, the residents of your society might have access to magic items that duplicate the effects of phones, automobiles, and similar modern conveniences.

entries.name: Laws
entries: Even a novice spellcaster, able to cast nothing more than a cantrip, can use their magic to kill. Powerful mages can secretly observe individuals from afar, probe the thoughts of others, or control minds. It stands to reason that magical societies would impose laws to restrict the use of invasive, coercive, and destructive magic.

When creating your magical world, consider how the law restricts the use of magic, if at all. Are mages punished only when their magic hurts others? Are certain spells always restricted, or does anything go?

entries.name: Outlawed Magic
entries: The simplest magic law is the strictest: a ban on all magic. Laws like this come about because a society has a long history of conflict with magical enemies, because magic is blamed for environmental or social ills, or because of simple superstition. Power-hungry mages who run a society might outlaw the use of magic by anyone other than the ruling class.

entries.name: Vilhon Reach
entries: Several regions of the Vilhon Reach in the Forgotten Realms curtail or ban magic, particularly magic used to charm or injure others.

entries.name: Focusing on the Crime
entries: Some magical societies consider laws against the use of magic unnecessary when existing laws already prohibit the harmful effects of magic. After all, murder is murder, whether the victim was killed with a sword, a spell, or the killer's bare hands.

For example, a large city like Greyhawk or Waterdeep might have laws against theft and laws that prohibit spying on a person in their home. An individual caught performing such acts would be guilty of a crime whether they cast the {@spell Invisibility|XPHB} spell or used nonmagical means.

Magic might count as an aggravating factor during sentencing, however. An individual found guilty of murder who killed the victim with the {@spell Finger of Death|XPHB} spell might be given a harsher sentence by a judge.

entries.name: Frontier Justice
entries: In remote regions that lack effective law enforcement, individuals and communities decide how magic and mages are treated. Residents might be suspicious of magic and intolerant of public spellcasting. Or they might become antagonistic toward mages who use magic in a way the residents don't like. As a third option, a single law enforcement official, such as a sheriff or marshal, might decide which mages are allowed to practice their craft undisturbed and which are driven out of town.

entries.name: Ten-Towns
entries: In the remote settlements of Ten-Towns in the Forgotten Realms, an innkeeper might hang up a "No Spells Allowed" sign and hire a bouncer or two to enforce this rule. Putting up such a sign is the innkeeper's right, but the town guard (if there is a town guard) is under no obligation to enforce it.

entries.name: Commerce
entries: How magic intertwines with commerce in your world is a key part of how your characters interact with it.

How easily can your characters find magic item shops or mages to purchase spellcasting services from? How accessible are magic items of higher rarity, such as Legendary magic items or Artifacts? Do mages' guilds regulate the accessibility of magic?

entries.name: Magic Item Shops

entries.title: Members of House Deneith in Eberron work as paid, magic-wielding bodyguards.

entries: While {@item Spell Scroll|XDMG|Spell Scrolls} and {@item Potion of Healing|XDMG|Potions of Healing} are included in gear a character can buy in the {@book Player's Handbook|XPHB}, the {@book Dungeon Master's Guide|XDMG} leaves it up to the DM to decide what magic items are available to purchase in a campaign. A variety of magic item shops might be common in your world.

If you want Rare or rarer magic items to feel special, treat them like antiquities or fine art. A magic item shop in such a setting could be owned and operated by a single person who has deep knowledge of magical lore and contacts all over the world. When an adventurer asks for a specific magic item, the shop owner can procure it eventually, but the search takes time and leads to an adventure.

If magic items are more common in your world, a magic item shop in a city might look more like a pawnshop. All kinds of magic items would line the shelves, including duplicates of especially useful items such as {@item Bag of Holding|XDMG|Bags of Holding}. The owner might be assisted by several individuals who specialize in security and deterring theft.

entries.name: Magical Businesses
entries: While any mage can sell their spellcasting services, your magical society might be filled with mages who use magic to earn a living in more interesting ways. The {@book Player's Handbook|XPHB} presents availability and cost details for spellcasting services, but you can alter this availability as best suits your world.

For example, a novice spellcaster who can cast the {@spell Prestidigitation|XPHB} spell could operate a laundry service, quickly and easily cleaning clothes. A chef could use the same spell to flavor food for an hour. Cantrips such as {@spell Elementalism|XPHB}, {@spell Guidance|XPHB}, {@spell Mending|XPHB}, and {@spell Spare the Dying|XPHB} are also well suited for a humble but reliable magical career.
Magical businesses could take dramatic forms in your setting. Eberron is full of examples, from the magical artificers of House Cannith to the magical bodyguards of House Deneith.

entries.name: Mages' Guilds
entries: A mages' guild is an alliance of mages who run a robust magical business in a city. Such guilds are a staple of fantasy roleplaying games, especially campaigns with roots in D&D's earliest editions and settings, such as Greyhawk.

entries.name: Guild Practices
entries: A successful mages' guild works hand in hand with the local law enforcement. Typically, local laws don't prohibit spellcasting or making magic items, but they prohibit those who don't belong to the guild from making a profit by providing services that fall under the guild's exclusive concerns.

The local law enforcement typically includes members who are mages—and members of the guild. Both the guild and law enforcement tend to spend considerable time and effort monitoring mages in the city, enforcing guild rules and looking for mages avoiding guild membership.

entries.name: Membership
entries: Mages in a guild enjoy a monopoly on magical commerce. They expect to be paid an agreed-on amount of money for their services. Further, the guild is an excellent place for networking with other mages, and it probably operates a guildhall that includes a library of magical tomes and spellbooks as well as dining facilities, sleeping areas, and more. A guildhall could serve as an excellent base of operations for a group of characters connected to the guild.
Guild members are expected to pay dues and obey the guild's rules. In this way, a mages' guild in your world could serve as your characters' employer—as well as their debt holder.

entries.name: Rank
entries: Membership in the guild might be structured into three or more ranks. While members of the lowest rank have no influence in the guild and are expected to assist senior members for little or no pay, high-ranking members enjoy a wealthy lifestyle, authority in the guild, and the assistance of lower-ranking members.

entries.name: Campaign Role
entries: A mages' guild can serve as a group patron for characters or as an adversary that must be overcome. As a patron, the guild offers access to spellbooks, a comfortable refuge from danger, and magical allies knowledgeable on numerous subjects.

But a mages' guild might instead be an oppressive organization that ruthlessly exploits its monopoly and harasses nonmembers. Your campaign could focus on ousting the guild's leaders and replacing them with egalitarian leadership.

entries.name: Magical Armies

entries.title: A War Wizard of Cormyr casts a powerful Evocation spell on the battlefield.

entries: Fantasy realms raise and maintain armies to defend their territories. A society steeped in magic might establish magical armies to complement its regular troops. What benefits do magical armies provide, and what forms do they take?

entries.name: War Wizards
entries: A magical army might boast mages in its ranks, either mixed in among ordinary soldiers or forming elite units composed entirely of spellcasters. The War Wizards of Cormyr in the Forgotten Realms is an archetypal example of this kind of elite unit.

War wizards defy mage stereotypes. They often wear armor and wield martial weapons, resembling Eldritch Knights. Alternatively, a war wizard might wear simple robes and wield a staff but focus on damaging spells. These mages function as mobile artillery units, protected by martial soldiers. {@creature Spellguard|AU|Spellguards} (see {@book chapter 6|AU|6}) might feature prominently in such an army.

entries.name: Magical Minions
entries: A magical army might supplement or even replace ordinary soldiers with magical minions. During the Last War, Eberron's armies extensively used magical minions, with the nation of Karrnath fielding armies of zombies and skeletons while Cyre and other nations used constructs. Outside Eberron, other magical realms fill their armies with conjured creatures or elementals summoned from the Inner Planes.

Fielding magical minions allows commanders and martial soldiers to remain safely behind the battle line while the minions participate in combat. A realm heavily dependent on magical minions might enter war more quickly than other realms and take more risks on the battlefield, brushing off the loss of magical minions as insignificant since they're easily replaced.

entries.name: Magical Fortifications
entries: A traditional castle isn't much of a defense against mages who can cast spells such as {@spell Fly|XPHB}, {@spell Passwall|XPHB}, and {@spell Teleport|XPHB}. Fortunately, a realm with magical resources has many magical ways to defend itself. Defensive measures such as the {@spell Wall of Force|XPHB}, {@spell Globe of Invulnerability|XPHB}, and {@spell Antimagic Field|XPHB} spells cover a small area for a limited time and are useful in emergencies. But options such as the {@spell Forbiddance|XPHB} and {@spell Guards and Wards|XPHB} spells last much longer and can provide layers of magical defenses. Entrances can be protected with the {@spell Glyph of Warding|XPHB} spell.

A fortification might be protected by magical defenders that negate an enemy's advantages. For example, flying assailants could be countered with flying defenders, such as soldiers mounted on griffins, hippogriffs, or pegasi.

entries.name: Mastering Magic

entries.title: In your world, magical instruction might involve hundreds of students learning from masters in an arena such as this one.

entries: If magic suffuses your world, consider how its inhabitants learn their magical craft. Is magic laboriously taught by an elderly expert to a single apprentice? Do aspiring mages enroll at an academy where they're taught alongside others? Or do novice spellcasters learn another way?

The forms of magical instruction can be described in four ways: solitary study, apprenticeship, academic instruction, or cultural immersion, where magical instruction is readily available to all. Most magical societies rely on a single type of magical instruction. You might decide, however, that different kinds of instruction are prevalent in different parts of the world. For example, a magical realm might boast a magical academy with hundreds of students, but in the realm's capital, magic might be so common that everyone knows a spell or two thanks to the cultural prevalence of magic in everyday life.

entries.name: Solitary Study
entries: When magic is learned through solitary study, each mage understands magic slightly differently. For example, one mage might conceive of magic as influenced by the stars and planets, while another conceptualizes magic as an imperceptible force that connects all things. Both mages can cast spells of equivalent strength and effect, but their understanding of the underlying origin of magic varies.

entries.name: Warlocks
entries: In a society that relies on solitary study, every mage is self-taught. Warlocks, who cobble together magical power from pacts and little-understood scraps of lore, are the most common kind of spellcaster in these societies. Wizards, who traditionally rely on learning from others, might be rare.

entries.name: Apprenticeship
entries: When magic is learned through apprenticeship, magical instruction is limited to one-on-one relationships between an expert and a novice. An experienced mage might have many apprentices in a lifetime but teach only one at a time. As a result, there are always more candidates for apprenticeship than mentors, and competition among potential apprentices might be intense. Experienced mages might screen candidates or develop elaborate tests for prospective apprentices, measuring their intelligence, loyalty, magical acumen, or ethical code. These tests might serve as low-level adventures in your world.

entries.name: Campaigns
entries: In a campaign focused on apprenticeship, the mentor becomes unusually important. Craft interesting mentors your players will enjoy interacting with. The archetypal mentor is enigmatic and seemingly omnipotent, but they can also be whimsical, grouchy, or absent-minded.

In addition to creating a memorable mentor, consider when and how your characters' apprenticeships end. Is a level 1 Wizard finished with their apprenticeship? Or do they remain an apprentice until level 3 or later? How does the mentor decide when the student has learned enough?

entries.name: Sorcerers
entries: Sorcerers flourish in societies focused on apprenticeship. Many sorcerers inherit their powers from a magical ancestor, or their powers might be shared among members of their family. These family connections make it easier to secure a mentor, and the family might have well-established traditions around recognizing, controlling, and mastering magic.

entries.name: Academic Instruction
entries: In a long-established magical society, the myriad magical philosophies taught by individual mentors eventually coalesce around the most successful teachers. When these teachers pool their resources to form a magical academy, large numbers of students can benefit from academic instruction. Styles of magical academies are further detailed in "{@area Magical Academies|16c|x}" below.

entries.name: Wizards
entries: Wizards flourish in a magical society with academic instruction. Dutifully showing up to school every day, books in hand, Wizards learn new spells in a classroom environment. During off hours, they practice magic, pursue magical interests on their own, and get into the sort of trouble students always find.

entries.name: Cultural Immersion
entries: Magic in your society might be so well understood and so widespread that aspiring mages can learn basic magic from everyday life. In such a society, books of magical instruction might be found at any bookstore or library. Everyone might know a spell or two, and learning a new one might be as easy as sitting down for a few hours with a friend and exchanging techniques. When magic is widely understood and a part of everyday life, you don't need to create magical academies or mentor figures to explain why characters know basic magic.

entries.name: Bards
entries: Bards—whose magic takes the form of music, dance, and other popular art forms—flourish in a society where magic is popular. To Bards, learning new magic might be as simple as overhearing a catchy tune in a tavern and reworking it for their own purposes.

entries.name: Magical Academies
entries: The magical academies in the worlds of D&D make useful models for your world-building. Consider the following when creating your magical academy.

entries.title: Magical academies sometimes have their own sports, such as the game of Mage Tower at Strixhaven.

entries.name: Everything Under One Roof
entries: The most common form of magical academy is a single place where several kinds of magic are taught. For example, Strixhaven, detailed in {@book Strixhaven: A Curriculum of Chaos|SCC}, is a magical academy where five different campuses teach opposing magic philosophies. Similarly, the Tower of High Sorcery in the Dragonlance setting, described in {@adventure Dragonlance: Shadow of the Dragon Queen|DSotDQ}, teaches that setting's three primary orders of magic.

An academy of this sort is home to mages with different philosophies, goals, and methods. These individuals are united around the higher goal of teaching magic to the next generation of students. A student at one of these academies has access to a wide variety of spells, magical traditions, and instructors. Because students come from far away, they benefit from interacting with people from all over the world.

This kind of academy provides players with a lot of character creation options. Characters of any background, species, class, or subclass might come together to study magic and are sent on adventures by teachers with competing agendas. A magical academy is an example of an esoteric institution group patron, detailed later in this chapter.

entries.name: Rival Academies
entries: A realm with a large population of aspiring mages might have multiple magical academies that each specialize in a different form of magic.

An academy of this sort might focus on a single kind of magic: for instance, magic from the Conjuration school, or bladesinging, an ancient elven technique of magical combat. Rivalries between such academies take forms ranging from athletic competitions to pranks, clandestine raids, or even physical violence.

Because all students at one such academy study a single kind of magic, the academy is less likely to function as the home base for your campaign. Instead, the rival academies likely feature in the backstories of characters who wield magic, serving as the source of the characters' early magical training. However, you might create a campaign in which graduates of these rival academies are brought together by a menace that threatens all the academies or even the entire realm.

entries.name: Magical Academies in the Real World
entries: In our world, old traditions speak of schools where eager students went to learn magic. Transylvanian legend describes the Scholomance, a school for sorcery where the devil taught ten students at a time. At the end of their term of instruction, nine students were allowed to depart, but the devil claimed the tenth. Other examples of magical academies in folklore include the Cave of Salamanca in Spain and Domdaniel, a magical school first mentioned in a French continuation of The Arabian Nights.

entries.name: Magical Group Patrons
entries: Whether your heroes wish to advance the agenda of a famous mage or seek access to a magical academy's ample resources, a group patron with significant magical prowess can create the cohesion that holds a campaign together and help your game feel infused with magic.
This section presents six types of magical group patrons around which you can create campaigns, as summarized on the Magical Patron Options table.

Each sample patron includes examples from the D&D multiverse and outlines for patronage campaigns. You can incorporate these into your game or use them as inspiration for your own magical group patron.
This section also explores the option of your group's patron hiding their identity for reasons benevolent or malign, which can be used with any of the group patrons that follow.

entries.caption: Magical Patron Options
rows: A powerful, often famous mage with clear goals that span the multiverse
An organization dedicated to education, research, or containing dangerous magic
A non-Humanoid mage or magical creature with a mysterious, timeless outlook
A group of powerful, like-minded mages deeply invested in political goals
A capricious individual with inscrutable motives and a malevolent or whimsical nature
An alliance of mages focused on pursuing a difficult goal or resolving a problem or threat

entries.name: How Patrons Work
entries: No matter their details, group patrons provide adventurers with some common benefits.

entries.name: Group Assistance
entries: Having a group patron gives an adventuring group a common purpose, which inspires better coordination in the form of guidance and encouragement. As a result of this connection, each member of your party can grant {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} on a {@variantrule D20 Test|XPHB} made by another member of the party. To grant {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} in this way, you and your target must be able to see or hear each other, and neither can have the {@condition Incapacitated|XPHB} condition. After granting {@variantrule Advantage|XPHB} in this way, you can't do so again until you finish a {@variantrule Long Rest|XPHB}.

entries.name: Perks
entries: Group patrons offer characters perks ranging from a steady wage to access to libraries and magical resources to unexpected allies. Specific perks are presented in the description of each group patron.

entries.name: Option: Make Your Patron Mysterious
entries: Concealing the true identity of your group patron can be a fun campaign linchpin, especially if your game involves magic-themed intrigue. Any of the magical group patrons described in this chapter might have reasons to stay anonymous. If you use a mysterious patron, create a strong reason the patron is hiding their identity.

entries.name: High-Profile Patron
entries: A group patron might remain anonymous because they're incredibly powerful, famous or infamous, or otherwise high profile, and their identity being known would undermine the characters' goals or ability to operate clandestinely. Or the patron might have reasons they wish to remain publicly unassociated with the characters. For example, perhaps the patron is a powerful political figure who can't publicly take sides in a civil dispute but wants the characters to side with freedom fighters over greedy merchants.

entries.name: Ulterior Motives

entries.title: Powerful patrons are eager to sponsor young heroes, but their intent is sometimes unclear.

entries: On the other hand, a patron might hide their identity because their motives are malevolent. The patron might try to trick the characters into performing deeds that destabilize a fragile peace or empower an evil overlord. Or a patron might remain anonymous because the characters would never knowingly work for them, especially if the patron is nefarious and the heroes are upstanding.
Kindness promotes peace and good, but the practicalities of the world require coin. A patron who supplies the latter is useful; a patron who also believes in you is invaluable.

entries.name: Concealing Their Identity
entries: Mysterious magical patrons don't show their true faces to the characters, communicating via anonymous letters, prearranged signals, and networks of underlings similarly unaware of the patron's identity. A mysterious patron might refer to themself with a code name that fits the nature of the missions they ask the characters to undertake. In this case, the characters can't gain benefits associated with the patron's identity, such as the archmage's and esoteric institution's Documentation perks or the magical entity's Name Drop perk. Instead, the characters must find ways other than invoking their patron's name to achieve their goals.

entries.name: Using Magic
entries: Since magical patrons are typically powerful mages, they use high-level spell effects to ensure the characters don't discover their identity. A patron might repeatedly use the {@spell Programmed Illusion|XPHB} spell to convey information to the characters via fictional, illusory agents. If a patron must interact with a character, the patron might use the {@spell Seeming|XPHB} spell to significantly alter their appearance. Similarly, a patron might use the {@spell Mirage Arcane|XPHB} spell to conceal their lair's true location behind an illusory waterfall or trees. As your characters gain power, ensure their patron uses magic that the characters are unlikely to dispel.

entries.name: Keeping the Characters on Board
entries: If you use a mysterious group patron in your game, it's important for the characters to remain convinced that the patron's goals align with theirs. Attribute to the patron's code name deeds that are benevolent or helpful to the characters. Or ensure the patron compensates the characters well for their work, giving the characters a practical reason to continue working for them.

entries.name: The Big Reveal
entries: Eventually, the novelty of being sponsored by a mysterious group patron will wear thin. The characters might lose interest in working for someone unwilling to reveal their identity. They might begin to distrust or become frustrated with the patron.
When the time is right, you might reveal the patron's identity. You can do so suddenly, with the patron meeting the characters in person to thank them for their work, or more subtly.

entries.name: Dropping Hints
entries: As the characters complete more of the patron's missions, the patron might begin to drop—intentionally or unintentionally—coded hints about their identity. Investigating these clues can become a fun side quest for the characters.

entries.name: Benevolent Patron
entries: Once the characters have solved the clues, the patron might appear in person to congratulate them on discovering the secret. The patron might have intended to reveal themself once the characters proved themselves worthy through solving the clues, or the characters might have preempted the patron's plans. Either way, this gradual approach provides satisfaction to characters eager to learn their patron's identity.

entries.name: Malevolent Patron
entries: If the patron's motives are malicious, the characters might react with horror to their patron's identity. In this case, providing a satisfying conclusion to your campaign involves the characters confirming their patron's identity and formulating a plan for dealing with them. That might involve leaving the patron's employ abruptly, turning the tables on the patron to discredit them, confronting the patron in combat, or another option.

Follow your players' lead in how to wrap up the campaign. You might decide that the patron anticipated the characters' realization, but keep in mind that defeating this duplicitous patron allows a satisfying conclusion.

entries.name: Archmage
entries: As incredibly powerful spellcasters, archmages are capable of impressive deeds. Beyond slaying dragons or destroying undead, archmages have saved (and ruled!) entire cities, driven back armies, defeated the forces of the {@book Nine Hells|XDMG|5|Nine Hells} or the {@book Abyss|XDMG|5|Abyss}, and traveled in time. The mightiest archmages achieve magical mastery over the physical world. Some no longer age, spending centuries amassing unfathomable magical knowledge and prowess and creating spells they name after themselves.

With archmages' great learning and magical capabilities comes even greater willpower. Standing among the multiverse's strongest personalities, archmages personify stubbornness (even among the best) and self-centeredness (prominent among the worst). This unyielding nature translates into a voracious drive, whether it's to protect the weak, combat the wicked, amass the most knowledge, or take the biggest risks.

entries.name: Archmage Motivations
entries: {@creature Archmage|XMM|Archmages} might patronize a group for the following reasons:

items.name: Emissaries Are Needed
items.entry: {@creature Archmage|XMM|Archmages} amass allies and commune with powerful leaders during their travels throughout the multiverse. An archmage hires the characters to travel to these allies and request their aid—or aid those allies—in the archmage's pursuit of friendly relations or magical research.

items.name: Evil Is Rising
items.entry: Benevolent archmages recognize the sheer power of unchecked evil and are sensitive to such forces amassing strength or plotting terrible deeds. An archmage who discovers complex and wicked schemes hires the characters to complete tasks that undermine those schemes.

items.name: Lieutenants Are Required
items.entry: An archmage who identifies numerous threats plaguing a certain area hires the characters to face a host of lesser threats so the archmage can focus on powerful villainous leaders.

entries.name: Archmage Patrons
entries: The following characters from the D&D multiverse could serve as archmage group patrons:

entries.title: Lady Alustriel Silverhand is a powerful archmage who patronizes groups in the Forgotten Realms and beyond.

items.name: Alustriel Silverhand
items.entry: One of the most powerful mages in the Forgotten Realms setting, Alustriel has been a proponent of good and enemy of evil for centuries. Alustriel is an immortal human daughter of Mystra, a god of magic, and ruled the city of Silverymoon for centuries. Alustriel maintains safe houses scattered across the planes for her allies as they promote compassion throughout the multiverse.

items.name: Vajra Safahr
items.entry: Chief mage of Waterdeep in the Forgotten Realms setting, the human Vajra is the youngest head in the history of Blackstaff Academy, a school for mages. While Vajra fends off threats to her city and her university, she also faces political conflicts from those who would unseat her from her place of prestige.

items.name: Yolande
items.entry: Known as the Faerie Queen, Yolande is the benevolent and beloved elf monarch of the nation of Celene in the world of Greyhawk. She is a mighty wizard who protects her nation against the incursion of Elemental Evil forces as well as threats against the Feywild and the Material Plane.

entries.name: Creating Your Own Archmage
entries: Instead of using one of the archmages described above, you can create an archmage to serve as a group patron for your characters. You might start by choosing one of the eight archmage stat blocks in chapter 6, each of which specializes in one school of magic, and add personality details as you see fit.

When creating an archmage, consider how close to the traditional archetype you want your archmage to be. A traditional archmage is incredibly powerful and eccentric. They're easily distracted because they're nurturing layers of complicated schemes. Your archmage could be very different: plain spoken, attentive to the characters, not as powerful as their reputation would suggest—or far more so.
When you create an archmage for your campaign, you can roll on or choose from the Archmage Type table to determine details of the archmage's persona.

entries.caption: Archmage Type
rows: Aspiring Tyrant. Secretly aspiring to immense political power, the archmage sends the characters on missions that covertly support the archmage's goal.

Disguised Sage. The archmage disguises themself as a humble apprentice of limited magical ability, while their loud and boastful student pretends to be the archmage. The two keep their true identities secret from the party.

Distracted Genius. The archmage lives in a secluded cottage in the middle of the forest and spends most of their time talking to animals and plants. They employ the characters to handle problems so the mage can spend more time on their harmless personal pursuits.

Forlorn Lover. Having lost the love of their life through hubris to rejection or death, the archmage is focused on winning that individual back or resurrecting them. They need the characters to take care of other problems in the meanwhile.

Redeemed Demonologist. Once a devotee of a demon prince or archdevil, the archmage has renounced evil. They want the characters to solve the problems created when the archmage abandoned their former patron while the archmage focuses on larger challenges.

Wizened Elf. The elf archmage is thousands of years old, their long life magically extended. The archmage remembers errors made over the centuries by well-meaning individuals and employs the characters to stop similar mistakes from happening again.

entries.name: Archmage Patron Perks
entries: Characters in a party whose patron is an archmage gain the following perks.

entries.name: Compensation
entries: {@creature Archmage|XMM|Archmages} amass considerable wealth during their adventures and travels, and archmage patrons generously compensate their underlings. The nature of your work for an archmage influences how you're paid. On average, the archmage pays each member of your group 2 GP per day (enough to sustain a {@book Comfortable|XPHB|6|Comfortable (2 GP per Day)} lifestyle). Or you might be paid (at least 300 GP) each time you complete a task the archmage assigns.

entries.title: Coins

entries.name: Documentation
entries: Each member of your group has identification noting their affiliation with the archmage, which carries clout in areas where the archmage is known. If the archmage is the ruler of a city or nation, the documentation grants the characters appropriate authority in that realm.

entries.name: Magical Resources
entries: {@creature Archmage|XMM|Archmages} collect untold magic items and magical curiosities, though these collections are often scattered among far-flung sanctums. An archmage can give you any Common or Uncommon magic item in the {@book Dungeon Master's Guide|XDMG}, as long as possession of the item would help your group's tasks. When your group reaches level 11, the archmage can retrieve one Rare and one Very Rare magic item in between the group's tasks and award it to you as additional compensation. When your group reaches level 17, the archmage can retrieve one Rare, Very Rare, or Legendary magic item in between tasks and award it to you as additional compensation.

entries.name: Spellcasting
entries: {@creature Archmage|XMM|Archmages} can use their spellpower to help your missions. An archmage can cast any level 1 or lower spell for you at no cost, as long as the spell's effects would aid your work. The archmage can cast any level 2–8 spell for you at half the usual cost.

entries.name: Archmage Contacts
entries: An archmage group patron might prioritize working with the characters, meeting with the party directly to deliver missions and collect reports. In this case, the archmage becomes a significant recurring character in your campaign, so give the archmage a manner of speaking or another feature that makes them distinctive. For example, the archmage might talk to their snake familiar, wear outrageously garish outfits, or hum odd tunes when distracted.

But archmages have a lot to do, and the patron might send a representative in their place. Roll on or choose from the Archmage Contact table to determine how the archmage interacts with the characters.

entries.caption: Archmage Contact
rows: Apprentice. A Humanoid apprentice relays messages to the characters. The apprentice might be harried, exceedingly proud, or exhausted and overworked.
{@spell Magic Mouth|XPHB}. The archmage sends messages through the {@spell Magic Mouth|XPHB} spell, casting it on objects that vanish once the message is delivered.

Magical Servant. The contact is a loyal servant creature. It might be a Beast or Plant awakened through the {@spell Awaken|XPHB} spell or a fantastical creature such as a {@creature Blink Dog|XMM}, a {@creature Couatl|XMM}, or a {@creature Flumph|XMM}.
Projected Illusion. The archmage communicates with the characters through the {@spell Project Image|XPHB} spell. The characters might never see the archmage in person.

Sentient Magic Item. A sentient weapon, helmet, or other magic item communicates with the characters on the archmage's behalf. The item is hundreds of years old and exasperated with the characters' mistakes, though it loves its archmage creator.
{@spell Simulacrum|XPHB}. The archmage uses the {@spell Simulacrum|XPHB} spell to create simulacra that issue instructions on the archmage's behalf.

entries.name: An Archmage Campaign
entries: A campaign driven by an archmage patron might unfold according to this outline:

items.name: Levels 1–4
items.entry: As the characters begin their adventuring career, the archmage watches them from afar, monitoring their activities and subtly directing their attention to the groundlings (see {@book chapter 6|AU|6}) that a wicked rival archmage commands.

items.name: Levels 5–10
items.entry: The archmage reveals themself to the characters and hires the characters to investigate the rival archmage, whose schemes threaten the city or surrounding realm. You can use the stat block for one of the archmages in chapter 6 for this rival, whom the party confronts in a climactic battle.

items.name: Levels 11–16
items.entry: The archmage patron sends the characters all over the world to gather magical secrets from creatures that hoard knowledge; adult dragons, devils, and a {@creature Demilich|XMM} make suitable antagonists.

items.name: Levels 17–20
items.entry: The archmage patron retires. The characters are now obliged to deal with the archmage's enemies and rivals while exploring the archmage's extraplanar lair.

entries.name: Esoteric Institution
entries: An esoteric institution might be a magical academy, an order of monks researching lost magical techniques, or any other organization focused on the study, preservation, and use of magical lore. Institutions usually maintain a base of operations such as a campus, monastery, or remote fortress. The institution might have a large staff including administrators, teachers, groundskeepers, and guards. In addition to an excellent library, it probably has a secure vault for storing dangerous magic items, and more than one Artifact might be housed there.

Esoteric institutions have a long history that stretches back generations. In that time, an institution has made enemies and collected magic items that have been stored away and forgotten. The institution's headquarters might have secret chambers protected by puzzles and traps. Despite its reclusive or insular nature, the institution monitors the world beyond its walls. When it finds magic being used for evil or learns of long-forgotten lore to be recovered, it sends adventurers on missions.

entries.title: The Tower of High Sorcery in the world of Dragonlance charges heroes with protecting magical secrets from a destructive draconic army.

entries.name: Esoteric Institution Motivations
entries: An esoteric institution might patronize a group for the following reasons:

items.name: The Characters Are Students
items.entry: The characters are students at an academy such as the Tower of High Sorcery in the Dragonlance setting or Strixhaven University and are sent on missions as part of their studies. The institution doesn't intentionally send the characters on dangerous missions, and it sends rescue teams if the characters get into trouble while pursuing goals tied to the academy.

items.name: The Institution Needs Field Agents
items.entry: An esoteric institution includes sages, scholars, and researchers, but few warriors and explorers. The institution wants to hire the characters for missions deemed too dangerous for its own staff, such as rescuing students in peril.

items.name: The Characters Are Specialists
items.entry: An esoteric institution seeks out the characters because the characters are experts in a particular field relevant to a current problem or interest. For example, if the characters recently defeated a powerful vampire, the institution hires them to recover that vampire's hidden library of magical tomes.

entries.name: Esoteric Institution Patrons
entries: The following organizations from the D&D multiverse could serve as esoteric institution group patrons:

items.name: Order of the Guardians
items.entry: The Order of the Guardians is a group of ascetics who gather, sequester, and protect dangerous magic in the Ravenloft setting. Its members maintain several hidden and well-protected monasteries, but the largest is Watchers' Stronghold in the Mistlands, a piece of the disintegrating domain of Darkon. The order is stretched thin, outnumbered and outmatched by the horrors found in the {@book Domains of Dread|XDMG|5|Domains of Dread}, and it's quick to hire adventurers willing to venture into dangerous sites to recover powerful items or spells so they can't be used for evil. More information on the Order of the Guardians and Darkon can be found in {@book Ravenloft: The Horrors Within|RHW}.

items.name: Thebestys
items.entry: In the Outlands of the Planescape setting, the walled city of Thebestys is home to an ibis-headed, many-named god of learning. This god maintains a great library at the city's center. The library enjoys a reputation as a matchless repository of knowledge. The ibis-headed god employs the characters as agents who travel through the city of {@book Sigil|XDMG|5|Sigil, City of Doors} and the planes to find books and bring them back to the library for copying and collection. Thebestys and the Outlands are detailed in {@book Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse|PAitM}.

items.name: Tower of High Sorcery
items.entry: In the Dragonlance setting, there were once five Towers of High Sorcery, where mages were trained. Due to disaster and tragedy, only one remains. There, spellcasters study magic in traditions tied to the world of Krynn's three moons. Characters in this setting serve the mages of the tower as teachers, students, or defenders, and they are dispatched to locations across the world to preserve magical secrets from the destructive draconian army. You can find more information on the Tower of High Sorcery in {@adventure Dragonlance: Shadow of the Dragon Queen|DSotDQ}.

entries.name: Creating Your Own Esoteric Institution
entries: Instead of using one of the esoteric institutions described above, you can create an institution to serve as a group patron for your characters. This gives you an opportunity to customize the institution to appeal to your players and to reflect the characters they've created. For example, if your players have made wilderness-oriented characters such as Barbarians, Druids, and Rangers, the institution you create is likely focused on preserving nature. If you want tension between the characters and the institution, the leaders of the institution might be of different alignments than the characters.
When you create an esoteric institution for your campaign, roll on or choose from the Esoteric Institution Type table to inspire the institution's details.

entries.caption: Esoteric Institution Type
rows: Apocalyptic Cult. This cult collects powerful magic lore and items to prepare for a world-ending battle the institution's leaders know is coming. These leaders don't tell the characters the full context of their plans, but they need the characters' help in preparing for the fight.

Magical Warehouse. This institution is dedicated to finding and hiding dangerous magic. It maintains a warehouse filled with anonymous crates, each containing a powerful magic item or tome of magical lore. The institution needs the characters to track down and recover dangerous items to store in the warehouse, which itself might be magical.

Military School. At this institution, mages train to serve in the realm's armed forces as officers and mobile artillery units. The institution emphasizes obedience, duty, and patriotism, and it needs disciplined characters to perform missions to ensure its longevity.

Religious Order. A religious order devoted to one or more gods of magic teaches spellcasting, performs religious rituals for the community, and pursues the gods' goals. The institution needs the characters to further these goals.

Underground Society. This informal network of aristocrats, mages, and scholars meets in inns, taverns, and other social venues to pursue clandestine schemes that might include sabotage, thievery, and mayhem. The institution needs discreet characters to perform delicate tasks.
University. Students from all over the world come to this famous university to study magic. The institution needs the characters to perform missions to preserve and further its reputation.

entries.name: Esoteric Institution Patron Perks
entries: Characters in a party whose patron is an esoteric institution gain the following perks.

entries.name: Compensation
entries: The institution pays for the work you do on its behalf. The nature of your employment influences your compensation. On average, the institution pays each member of your group 1 GP per day (or enough to sustain a {@book Modest|XPHB|6|Modest (1 GP per Day)} lifestyle). Or you might be paid a bounty (at least 250 GP) for each magic item or piece of lore you bring back from your adventures and give to the institution.

entries.name: Documentation
entries: Each member of your group has identification noting their affiliation with the institution, which carries clout in areas where the institution is known. For magical academies such as the Tower of High Sorcery or Strixhaven, this is a letter on official stationery marked with the academy's seal, but for secretive organizations like the Order of the Guardians, the documentation takes the form of a signet ring or brooch marked with a discreet symbol.

entries.name: Esoteric Research
entries: Esoteric institutions include expansive libraries specializing in magical knowledge. When you take a {@book Bastion|XDMG|7|Gaining a Bastion} turn, you can (as a group) issue the Research order to the institution as if it were a {@facility Library|XDMG} facility in your Bastion. The topic chosen must be related to magic in some way; at the DM's discretion, the institution can research topics related to the planes as well. Once you reach level 13, you instead can issue the Research order to the institution as if it were an {@facility Archive|XDMG}.

entries.name: Scroll and Spellbook Access
entries: You have access to the institution's library of {@item Spell Scroll|XDMG|Spell Scrolls} and spellbooks, as well as supplies for copying spells. You can buy any {@item Spell Scroll|XDMG} from the institution for half its usual value, as indicated in the {@book Dungeon Master's Guide|XDMG}. You can find any spell from the Player's Handbook in the library, and the institution pays half the GP cost of copying the spell.

entries.name: Training
entries: You have access to continuing education at no cost. You can spend 30 days in classes to gain one of the following benefits of your choice:

items.name: Skill
items.entry: You gain proficiency in one of these skills of your choice: {@skill Arcana|XPHB}, {@skill History|XPHB}, {@skill Nature|XPHB}, or {@skill Religion|XPHB}. You can gain proficiency in only one skill in this way.

items.name: Tool
items.entry: You gain proficiency with a tool of your choice.

items.name: Language
items.entry: You learn a language of your choice.

entries.name: Esoteric Institution Contacts
entries: An esoteric institution is typically large enough that the characters don't know everyone in it, and its leaders are too busy to interact with the characters directly. Usually, one individual is the party's contact, passing on instructions from the institution.

Think carefully about the contact's personality, because your players will interact with them often. The contact doesn't have to stay the same throughout the campaign; the institution might assign a new contact every mission or only in extreme circumstances.
Roll on or choose from the Esoteric Institution Contact table to determine who manages the relationship between the characters and the institution.

entries.caption: Esoteric Institution Contact
rows: Administrative Assistant. This polished professional has served the institution for decades, seems to know everything, and brooks no arguments.
Anonymous Mail. The characters get their missions via couriers sent by the institution. The group patron might be a single individual pretending to speak for the entire institution.
Mascot. A highly intelligent creature beloved by the staff bonds with the party and serves as an adviser and guide.
New Hire. Newly hired, the contact is inexperienced and can't answer the party's questions without consulting their superiors, but they're well meaning and sincere.
Overeager Graduate Student. This idealistic, advanced student idolizes the party and supports their every action.
Senior Faculty Member. The most famous member of the institution personally delivers all missions and takes great interest in the party's activities.

entries.name: An Esoteric Institution Campaign
entries: A campaign driven by an esoteric institution patron might unfold according to this outline:

items.name: Levels 1–4
items.entry: The characters begin as students at an esoteric institution where they study magic. Their early adventures involve exploring the institution (overcoming animated objects and other guardians) and the surrounding region (perhaps populated by modrons, myconids, or undead). As part of their graduation exam, the characters are tasked to defeat a {@creature Bulette|XMM} that threatens a nearby village.

items.name: Levels 5–10
items.entry: Now graduates of the institution, the characters are sent on missions to dangerous, far-off places where magical lore is hidden or being used for evil. They battle cultists of an evil god of magic and infiltrate the lair of a young dragon or a nest of {@creature Mind Flayer|XMM|mind flayers}.

items.name: Levels 11–16
items.entry: Eventually the characters are offered senior positions at the institution, where they become teachers of a new generation of pupils. They must defend the institution against enemies such as {@creature Arcanaloth|XMM|Arcanaloths}, {@creature Rakshasa|XMM|Rakshasas}, and a {@creature Vampire Umbral Lord|XMM}.

items.name: Levels 17–20
items.entry: At the climax of the campaign, a traitorous member of the esoteric institution steals an item the party recovered earlier and tries to use it to attain vast power or simple vengeance. The traitor is being manipulated by a {@creature Pit Fiend|XMM}, and only the characters can stop them.

entries.name: Magical Entity
entries: A magical entity is a powerful creature of mysterious or otherworldly origin. The entity might openly rule the realm in which they live, or they might be a mysterious figure that manipulates events from behind the scenes. Regardless, the magical entity is old, extremely knowledgeable, and frightening.

The magical entity is surrounded by legends and superstition. Villagers and townsfolk in the region know the entity by name. Most magical entities are feared as monsters, even if they're benevolent, though some are revered as honorable creatures that protect the realm.

entries.name: Magical Entity Motivations
entries: Magical entities might patronize a group for the following reasons:

items.name: Bound to a Place
items.entry: The magical entity is bound to a particular location and can't leave. While supremely powerful and all but omniscient in their own realm, the being needs the characters to accomplish objectives beyond the entity's reach.

items.name: Like Recognizes Like
items.entry: The magical entity sees something in the characters that reminds the entity of themself. A good patron likely admires heroes who are kind and just, while an evil patron might be impressed by characters they perceive as proud and cruel.

items.name: Too Famous to Travel
items.entry: The magical entity is so well known—and feared—that they can't travel without attracting unwanted attention and alerting their enemies. The entity needs agents who can avoid notice.

entries.name: Magical Entity Patrons

entries.title: Bahamut, a patron of good dragons, enlists heroes to fight against terrible evils.

entries: The following beings from the D&D multiverse could serve as magical entity patrons:

items.name: Baba Yaga
items.entry: An arch-hag known as the Mother of All Witches, Baba Yaga travels the multiverse in her chicken-legged hut, pursuing inscrutable goals. She's also the adoptive mother of the famous witch {@book Tasha|XDMG|8|Tasha}. Baba Yaga might hire characters of all alignments to seek esoteric magical knowledge or to act as her emissaries in formal political environments. Her goals and motivations are mysterious, but she offers great power to those she favors.

items.name: Bahamut
items.entry: {@book Bahamut|XDMG|8|Bahamut} is a god of good in numerous settings and is like a king to metallic dragons. He appears to mortals in various guises, often accompanied by seven yellow canaries that are gold dragons in disguise. In the world of Dragonlance, he has appeared as Fizban the Fabulous, a bumbling mage whose dramatic "accidents" often have hidden purposes.
